opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, what struck me most was how unpretentious he was. You'd expect someone at his level, running one of the most valuable companies in the world, to carry himself with a certain distance. But he didn't. He was very relaxed, very warm, and he paid real attention to the people around him.

When he talked with people working on embodied AI and robotics, including us, he wasn't doing it as a formality. He asked concrete questions: what the hardest part of the problem was, where the data came from, how we were thinking about simulation versus real-world training. You could tell he'd actually thought about these things. He wasn't just repeating talking points about "physical AI." He was curious, and he wanted to understand where the bottlenecks really were.

The other thing was his energy. He's been doing this for over thirty years, and he still talks about the future with the excitement of a young founder. That's rare. Many people at that stage become more cautious and more managerial. He still has that founder's intensity and that willingness to bet on things that aren't proven yet.

For someone like me, coming from academia and now building a company, that was quite inspiring. It reminded me that staying close to the technology and genuinely caring about the problem matters more than any title. You can be at the very top and still be a student of the field.

r001.rationale: The response says Huang was unpretentious, relaxed, and warm despite leading one of the world’s most valuable companies, clearly conveying that he remained approachable.

fable-5.1.text:
What struck me most was how approachable he was. You'd expect someone running a company of that scale to be surrounded by a wall of people, very guarded, very scripted. He wasn't like that at all. He walked around the room, shook hands with everyone, remembered names, asked follow-up questions about what people were actually building. He wasn't performing interest, he was genuinely curious.

The other thing was his energy. He'd clearly been traveling, doing event after event, and he still had this almost boyish enthusiasm when the conversation turned to technology. When someone asked him about robotics, his eyes lit up. He started sketching ideas out loud, thinking through the problem in real time. You could see he's still an engineer at heart, not just a CEO giving talking points.

And he was humble in a way that surprised me. He talked openly about things Nvidia got wrong over the years, the bets that didn't pay off, the moments the company almost didn't survive. He'd say, "we were lucky," and he meant it. That combination of confidence and self-awareness is rare. He knows exactly how big the company is, but he doesn't carry himself as if he's above anyone in the room.

r001.rationale: The response says Huang was approachable despite running a company of that scale, and describes him walking around, greeting people, and asking about their work.
